question: Will the UK increase the qualifying period for settlement to 10 years before May 2026?
summary: There is strong policy momentum toward a 10-year ILR baseline under Earned Settlement with rollout signals in 2026.
Adversarial objections identify timing risks: primary legislation, transitional rules, and potential political pushback could push implementation past May 2026.
Carve-outs and phased rollout reduce universal near-term adoption risk but do not negate the baseline.
Given timing risks, the near-term probability is calibrated below the ensemble, but still high for new applicants by May 2026.

justification.critique_assessment: Objections are valid and reveal a genuine timing and transitional risk that could prevent full adoption by May 2026.
justification.adjustment: Adjusted downward from the ensemble due to legislative/implementation timing risk and transitional complexities; the range captures remaining uncertainty about whether the policy will be implemented in time for new applicants by May 2026.

forecasts.reference-class: Earned settlement framework for UK settlement (ILR) policy: baseline 10-year qualifying period with potential reductions based on contributions; phased implementation starting April 2026

sources.claim: Public consultation Nov 2025–Feb 2026; baseline qualifying period proposed to be 10 years.
A Fairer Pathway to Settlement; the consultation document detailing the earned settlement model with a 10-year baseline and time-adjustment framework.
House of Commons Library briefing noting proposals to increase permanent residence to 10 years with implementation planned from April 2026.
Accessible version of the earned settlement consultation outlining the 10-year baseline and possible adjustments.
The default baseline qualifying period for settlement will be increased from 5 years to 10 years under an earned settlement model, with a public consultation on how reductions might apply.
The government announced a major overhaul of the legal migration model, including doubling the permanent settlement qualifying period to 10 years, with transitional considerations.
The Home Secretary announced a proposed contribution-based settlement model requiring a minimum of 10 years in the UK, with a consultation to follow.
Explanatory memorandum notes policy context and changes to settlement rules, including conversations around longer qualifying periods and earned settlement concepts.
The November 2025 earned settlement consultation outlines the 10-year baseline and potential adjustments based on contribution, integration, and other criteria.
Long residence route recognizes 10 years of lawful, continuous residence as a basis for settlement; updated guidance published in 2024.

MHA notes a Home Office consultation on 'Earned Settlement' closing Feb 12, 2026, proposing to raise the standard qualifying period for settlement from 5 to 10 years and outlining potential reductions.

Electronic Immigration Network reports the Home Office consultation on doubling the ILR qualifying period to 10 years (15 years for lower-skilled) with responses due by Feb 12, 2026; implementation could begin as early as April 2026.

Migration Observatory analysis indicates the baseline ILR wait would rise to 10 years with carve-outs; reductions possible for integration and contribution measures; changes subject to public consultation.
IPPR warns that hundreds of thousands of children could face a 10-year wait for settled status under the proposed settlement reforms.
Media coverage notes government plans to extend the ILR waiting period toward 10 years for many migrants as part of a broad immigration reform package.
FT analysis discusses potential impacts of the reforms, including effects on families and dependants, as well as the broader policy rationale.

synthesis: The objections reveal real timing and transitional design risks that plausibly delay near-term adoption, though official materials indicate a 10-year baseline with potential April 2026 rollout. Calibrating downward from the ensemble to reflect these risks yields a final probability around 0.85 with a 0.75–0.95 range for May 2026 implementation for new applicants.
